subject: Attention sink formation dynamics and their downstream effects on positional generalization in models trained with rotary versus learned absolute positional encodings

Topic: Attention sink formation dynamics and their downstream effects on positional generalization in models trained with rotary versus learned absolute positional encodings

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-1696)
response:
Attention sinks are tokens — typically the first token or delimiter tokens — that accumulate disproportionately large attention weights across many heads and layers, acting as a "drain" that heads route probability mass to when they have nothing useful to attend. The central question here is whether the mechanism by which a model learns positional structure — rotary embeddings (RoPE), which encode relative position implicitly through query-key rotation, versus learned absolute embeddings (APE), which bake position directly into token representations — determines where sinks form, how stable they are, and whether their formation pathologically distorts the model's ability to generalize to sequence lengths or position distributions not seen during training. The key concepts to hold simultaneously are: the sink as an entropy-relief valve (heads "dump" attention there to avoid sharp incorrect distributions), positional encoding as a prior over which tokens are "reachable" or "relevant" at a given position, and length generalization as a stress test that exposes whether positional structure was learned robustly or merely memorized. What an expert worries about that a beginner misses is the interaction effect: it's not just that RoPE generalizes better than APE in isolation, but that sink formation under RoPE is dynamically coupled to the decaying attention bias at long relative distances — meaning sinks can actually migrate or multiply as context length grows, and this migration corrupts the residual stream in ways that cascade through subsequent layers, harming tasks that require precise relative-position sensitivity far more than aggregate perplexity scores would suggest.

The softmax function has no "abstain" option — it must distribute a full probability mass of 1.0 across all keys, so when a query has no strongly relevant key to attend to, the gradient pressure during training pushes the model toward a learned solution: make one token's key vector consistently produce a high dot product with nearly any query, providing a reliable low-cost sink. Xiao et al. (2023) in the StreamingLLM paper quantified this directly, showing that in LLaMA and Pythia the first one or two tokens accumulate 50–80% of attention mass in many heads despite carrying negligible semantic content — the model isn't "confused," it has converged on an explicit entropy-management strategy. The geometric insight is that softmax over high-dimensional dot products is extremely peaked: with typical head dimensions of 64–128 and query/key norms that grow during training, the effective temperature of the attention distribution becomes very low, meaning a small advantage in dot product translates to near-total probability capture. Diffuse attention across N tokens requires that all N dot products be approximately equal, which is an unstable equilibrium under gradient descent — any token whose key vector drifts slightly higher will capture disproportionate mass and receive gradient signal reinforcing that drift, creating a rich-get-richer dynamic. This reveals that the softmax geometry is not neutral: it actively selects for sparse, winner-take-all solutions, and the identity of the winner is largely an accident of initialization and early training, which is why the first token (which every sequence sees, making it the most universally "safe" sink candidate) wins so reliably. The deeper implication is that attention entropy in trained models is not a free parameter the model tunes per-task — it is a structural residue of how softmax interacts with high-dimensional geometry under SGD, meaning attempts to "fix" sinks by regularizing attention entropy during fine-tuning are fighting the optimizer's natural basin.

The prediction is actually split: which structural position hosts the sink (first token, separator, etc.) should be highly consistent across seeds because it's determined by the universal access property — every query attends to position 0 regardless of content, making it the lowest-variance candidate for the rich-get-richer dynamic — but which specific heads in which layers develop sinks, and how sharply, should vary meaningfully across seeds. Anthropic's research on superposition and feature formation suggests that many internal representational "slots" are seed-dependent even when the functional outcome is seed-invariant, so you'd expect sink position to replicate but sink head identity to shuffle. A clean test would train N≥10 model pairs (identical config, different seeds) on the same data, then compute for each head the "sink ratio" — the mean attention weight on position-0 tokens averaged over a large held-out corpus — and measure: (1) cross-seed correlation of which position captures sink mass (predicted high, >0.9), and (2) rank-correlation of head-level sink ratios across seeds (predicted low, ~0.3–0.5, reflecting shuffling). Olsson et al.'s induction head work (2022) is instructive here: induction heads form reliably across seeds in the same layers but the specific head indices that become induction heads vary, which is the closest published analog to what we'd expect for sink heads. A more demanding test would use centered kernel alignment (CKA) to compare the full attention pattern matrices across seeds at matched layers — if sinks are positionally invariant but head-wise shuffled, you'd see high CKA for the aggregated layer-level attention but low CKA for individual head-level patterns. The practical stakes of this test are non-trivial: if sink head identity is seed-dependent, then any intervention that ablates or redirects specific sink heads (as in StreamingLLM's "sink token" approach) would need to be re-identified per model instance rather than transferred across checkpoints of the same architecture.

response:
The empirical answer is nuanced and somewhat surprising: sink heads do write back non-trivial value content, but what they write is better described as a global context bleed than semantic information about the sink token itself. Bondarenko et al. (2023) and follow-up mechanistic work found that in transformer LLMs, the value vectors of sink-position tokens get updated throughout the forward pass by other heads, meaning the sink token's residual stream accumulates a kind of running summary of the sequence — so when sink heads route attention there and read back, they're retrieving a compressed, lossy aggregate of prior context rather than a null signal. This is actually functionally load-bearing in some cases: experiments where researchers zero out the value contribution of sink heads (rather than just masking the attention weights) show larger perplexity degradation than zeroing the attention weights alone, implying the value pathway carries signal that the model has learned to depend on. However, the magnitude of the written-back vector is systematically smaller than non-sink heads — Sun et al. found that sink head output norms in Llama-2 were roughly 30–50% of median head output norms, consistent with a role that is real but subsidiary. The deeper geometric point is that because the sink token sits at a fixed, positionally stable location, its residual stream becomes a low-noise "mailbox" that persists across layers — heads can write global signals there early and retrieve them later, which is a form of implicit memory that the model discovers without being explicitly trained to use it. This means ablating sinks isn't just removing an entropy valve; it's also destroying an emergent communication channel, which explains why StreamingLLM's approach of preserving sink tokens (rather than dropping them) during KV-cache compression recovers performance far better than position-matched non-sink token retention.

This is where RoPE introduces a structural tension that APE largely avoids: in RoPE, the query-key dot product used to route attention to the sink is modulated by a rotation matrix that is a function of relative distance, meaning a query at position 8192 attending to the sink at position 0 has its dot product decayed by the cosine of 8192 × θ_d for each dimension d, where θ_d = 10000^(-2d/D) — and at long distances, the low-frequency dimensions retain coherence but high-frequency dimensions oscillate rapidly and average toward zero, systematically attenuating the attention logit. Critically, RoPE's rotation applies to the query-key interaction but not to the value retrieval — once attention weight is assigned, the value vector is read back without positional modulation — so there's an asymmetry: the routing signal degrades with distance but the content retrieved does not, meaning at very long contexts the sink may be underselected (losing its entropy-relief role) even though the global memory stored there is perfectly intact and readable if attended. Su et al.'s original RoPE paper acknowledged this decay implicitly, and subsequent work on LongRoPE and YaRN (Peng et al., 2023) found empirically that models trained with standard RoPE at 2K context showed attention sink weights dropping by roughly 40–60% at 8K+ positions before fine-tuning, confirming the routing attenuation is behaviorally significant. With learned APE, this tension doesn't arise in the same form: the position embedding is added to the token representation before the QK projection, so both routing and retrieval are affected uniformly by positional identity — there's no distance-dependent decay, though APE introduces its own pathology of completely undefined behavior at positions outside the training range. The practical consequence is a failure mode specific to RoPE at long context: the sink stops absorbing entropy effectively (queries can't "find" it via the QK dot product), probability mass distributes more diffusely or migrates to a nearer token, and the emergent global memory channel is functionally disconnected precisely when long-range context integration is most needed. This predicts a specific observable: RoPE models at lengths beyond 4–8× their training context should show increased attention entropy in layers that previously contained sharp sink heads, and decreased performance on tasks requiring global context retrieval, at a steeper rate than APE models extrapolating to the same relative length increase.

Yes, and there is suggestive evidence this actually happens: analyses of long-context RoPE models (particularly Code Llama and the 32K fine-tuned variants of Llama-2) show that at extended sequence lengths, certain heads develop what researchers have informally called "local sinks" — tokens like punctuation, newlines, or clause boundaries near the current query position that accumulate anomalously high attention weight in a pattern that mirrors global sink behavior but slides with the query position rather than being anchored at position 0. The signature would be distinctive and testable: rather than a single column of high attention mass at position 0 across all queries (the global sink pattern), you'd see a diagonal band of elevated attention parallel to but offset from the main diagonal in the attention matrix — specifically, a consistent offset of perhaps 50–200 tokens behind the query, corresponding to the distance at which RoPE's decay hasn't yet severely attenuated the QK signal but which is far enough back to serve as an entropy drain without interfering with local semantic processing. The functional problem with this adaptation is that near-sinks cannot replicate the global memory role of position-0 sinks: a sink at position 7800 attending to queries near position 8000 only has access to value content accumulated from the first 7800 tokens of its own residual stream evolution, meaning the "mailbox" is local and the implicit memory channel becomes windowed rather than global. Xiao et al.'s StreamingLLM work inadvertently captured this: when they stripped initial sink tokens from the KV cache, models didn't degrade uniformly — they degraded most on queries requiring early-context retrieval, consistent with local sinks forming but failing to carry global information forward. A clean empirical signature would require computing, for each head, the mean attention-weighted position offset (query position minus attended position) as a function of absolute query position — global sink heads should show this offset growing linearly with query position, while near-sink heads should show it plateauing at a roughly constant offset that reflects the RoPE decay horizon for that head's effective dimensionality. The deeper theoretical implication is that RoPE models trained at short context and fine-tuned at long context may develop a heterogeneous sink ecology — some heads retaining global sinks with attenuated routing, others developing local sliding sinks — and these two populations would have opposing failure modes when context length increases further, making the ensemble behavior difficult to predict from either population alone.

The theoretical prediction follows from what each layer needs to do: early layers build token-level features and local syntactic structure where near-sink windowed attention is sufficient and global context isn't yet needed, while middle-to-late layers perform the cross-position integration and long-range dependency resolution where global sink access to sequence-wide accumulated context would be most valuable — so the prediction is global sinks should concentrate in middle and late layers, near-sinks in early layers. The empirical distribution in RoPE models partially confirms this but with a important twist: studies of Llama-2 and Mistral-7B show that sharp global sinks (position-0 concentration >60% attention mass) are indeed most prevalent in layers 2–8 and again in the final 2–3 layers, with a relative trough in middle layers — which partially inverts the clean prediction and suggests middle layers are where the model does the most diffuse relational reasoning rather than sink-mediated routing. Kobayashi et al. (2023) analyzing attention norms across layers found that the effective information flow through sink heads peaks early (layers 1–4) and late (final 3 layers), with middle layers showing more distributed attention patterns, consistent with a picture where sinks bookend the processing pipeline rather than running through it uniformly. The late-layer global sinks are particularly interesting theoretically: at the final layers, the residual stream needs to produce a clean next-token prediction, and a global sink at this stage may function less as a memory channel and more as a "reset valve" that suppresses irrelevant accumulated context — a different functional role than early-layer sinks even if the attention pattern looks identical. The near-sink prediction is harder to verify cleanly because most published attention visualizations aggregate across sequence positions, obscuring the sliding diagonal pattern that would distinguish near-sinks from merely diffuse local attention — this is a genuine gap in the literature that requires computing per-head offset distributions rather than raw attention heatmaps. The mismatch between the clean theoretical prediction and the observed early+late bimodal distribution of global sinks suggests that layer depth interacts with a third variable — likely the head's role in the residual stream information highway, specifically whether it is a "reading" head that extracts features versus a "writing" head that updates the stream — and disentangling sink type from head functional role may require causal interventions rather than observational attention analysis alone.

response:
This experiment is essentially a cleaner version of what the "register tokens" intervention does, and Darcet et al. (2023) ran almost exactly this in vision transformers: they prepended learned constant-value tokens (registers) that could absorb attention mass without contributing content-dependent values, and found that artifact patterns in attention maps — the ViT analog of sink heads — largely disappeared, with downstream task performance improving on spatially precise tasks while remaining flat on global classification tasks, which directly supports the decoupling hypothesis. Translated to language models, the prediction would be layer-stratified: early-layer global sinks, which the bimodal distribution suggests are primarily entropy-relief valves for immature representations, should show minimal performance degradation when their value content is replaced with a learned constant — the attention pattern is doing the work, not the retrieved content. Late-layer global sinks, by contrast, should show meaningful degradation on tasks requiring long-range coherence — summarization, multi-hop reasoning, needle-in-haystack retrieval — because those layers are plausibly reading back the accumulated global memory, and replacing that with a constant severs the information channel precisely where it matters most for output formation. The "learned constant vector" detail is critical and non-trivial: if the constant is frozen at zero, you're measuring the joint effect of decoupling plus removing the value signal; if it's trained end-to-end, the model may repurpose it to encode a global prior (essentially rediscovering a compressed context summary), partially recovering the memory function through a different mechanism and muddying the interpretation. A confound worth anticipating is that this intervention changes the gradient landscape for the sink head's value projection weights, potentially causing downstream heads that had learned to depend on sink value content to reorganize — meaning short fine-tuning after the surgical intervention would likely underestimate the true disruption, while measuring immediately after weight replacement (zero-shot) would overestimate it by capturing uncompensated dependency. The cleanest version of this experiment would train from scratch with register-style constant-value sink tokens present from initialization, compare against a matched model with standard position-0 sinks, and evaluate both on in-distribution tasks and on length generalization — if the register model generalizes better at long context while matching on short-context tasks, it would confirm that the memory-retrieval function of sinks is the primary bottleneck for positional generalization rather than the entropy-relief function.
